prompt: What is the main job of `terraform.tfstate`?
hint: Look at what each entry pairs together.

choices.text: To store the provider binaries Terraform downloaded
choices.why: Providers live under `.terraform/`; the state holds none of them.

choices.text: To pair each address in the configuration with the id AWS gave it
choices.why: Yes: `aws_vpc.shop` beside the `vpc-…` id AWS invented. Nothing else holds both.

choices.text: To keep a log of every command Ana typed
choices.why: It records the result of applies, not a history of commands.

choices.text: To cache plans so the next one runs faster
choices.why: That is the belief the lesson corrects: the state is not a cache, and it cannot be rebuilt.

prompt: Two state files have the same `lineage`, one with `serial` 4 and one with `serial` 9. What does that say?
hint: One of the two numbers names a history, the other a point in it.

choices.text: They belong to two unrelated configurations that happen to match
choices.why: Unrelated states would have different lineages.

choices.text: The one with serial 9 was written by a newer Terraform version
choices.why: That is `terraform_version`; the serial counts writes.

choices.text: One history; serial 9 is five writes newer
choices.why: Right. Same lineage means the same history, and the serial goes up by one per write.

choices.text: Serial 9 holds nine resources
choices.why: The serial is a counter of writes, not of resources.

prompt: Why does Terraform not find `aws_vpc.shop` on each plan by searching for its `Name` tag?
hint: Lesson 1 created something that answers this.

choices.text: Tags are not readable through the EC2 API
choices.why: They are; `describe-vpcs` filtered on one in lesson 1.

choices.text: Because a name matches any number of VPCs, and an id names exactly one
choices.why: Yes. Two VPCs called `shop` existed at once; only an id names exactly one.

choices.text: Searching by tag costs more API calls than AWS allows per minute
choices.why: Rate limits are not the reason; one search is one call.

choices.text: Tag searches are slower than reading the file
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; ambiguity is.

prompt: In the fresh clone with no state, how many resources did `terraform plan` want to add?
hint: Count what `main.tf` declares.

prompt: The clone's apply created a second VPC and a second security group called `web`. Why did AWS not refuse the second group?
hint: Where does a security group's name have to be unique?

choices.text: Its name has to be unique inside its own VPC, and this one is in the new VPC
choices.why: Right, and the second group was created in the second VPC.

choices.text: Moto skips the uniqueness checks that real AWS performs
choices.why: Real AWS would accept it too; the rule is per VPC.

choices.text: Terraform renamed it with a random suffix
choices.why: Both are called `web`, as the listing shows.

choices.text: The first group had been deleted by the plan
choices.why: A plan changes nothing, and the first group is still listed.

prompt: A colleague deletes the duplicate's directory, state included, before anybody runs `destroy` in it. What is the situation now?
hint: Which state knew the duplicate?

choices.text: Ana's directory sees the extra VPC and offers to destroy it
choices.why: Her state knows only its own three ids; the duplicate is not in it.

choices.text: AWS removes the duplicate once nothing manages it
choices.why: AWS keeps what it was told to create, managed or not.

choices.text: Terraform merges the two networks on Ana's next apply
choices.why: Terraform never merges resources; it reads ids it already holds.

choices.text: The duplicate stays real and billed, and nothing manages it any more
choices.why: Yes. Telling it apart from the original now means reading ids by hand, or importing (lesson 8).

prompt: What does `terraform state rm aws_subnet.public_a` do to the subnet in AWS?
hint: The `describe-subnets` after it answers this.

choices.text: Deletes it, then removes it from the state
choices.why: That is `destroy`; `state rm` never calls AWS to delete.

choices.text: Marks it for replacement on the next apply
choices.why: That is `-replace` (lesson 6); `rm` makes Terraform forget it.

choices.text: Moves it to a backup state in the same directory
choices.why: A backup of the whole state is written, but the subnet itself is untouched.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: the subnet stays in AWS, and only the state forgets it.

prompt: After `state mv aws_subnet.a aws_subnet.public_a`, but before editing `main.tf`, what did the plan propose?
hint: The file and the state now disagree about a name.

choices.text: No changes, because the subnet's id did not change
choices.why: The id is fine; the address in the file and in the state differ.

choices.text: To destroy `public_a` and create a new `a` in its place
choices.why: Yes: `1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy`, a replacement caused by a name.

choices.text: To rename the subnet's `Name` tag to `public_a`
choices.why: Addresses are Terraform's names; they never reach a tag.

choices.text: An error, because `public_a` is not in the configuration
choices.why: It is not an error: a state entry with no configuration is planned for destruction.

prompt: To see what `terraform state mv` would do without changing anything, add the flag ___.
hint: A rehearsal flag.

prompt: Match each command to what it does.
hint: One right-hand item belongs to no command here.

pairs.right: Prints every address the state holds
Changes an address, keeping the object
Forgets an object without deleting it

right_distractors: Deletes the real resource and its entry

prompt: What did the ordinary `terraform plan` propose for the port 22 rule a colleague added by hand?
hint: Which side does a normal plan try to make AWS match?

choices.text: To write the rule into `main.tf`
choices.why: Terraform never edits the configuration; a person does.

choices.text: Nothing: rules added outside Terraform are ignored
choices.why: With inline `ingress` blocks the resource owns the whole list, so the extra rule is a difference.

choices.text: To remove it
choices.why: Yes, an update in place with the rule's lines marked `-`.

choices.text: To replace the whole security group
choices.why: It was `~ update in-place`, `1 to change`, not a replacement.

prompt: What does `terraform apply -refresh-only` change?
hint: Refresh reads; which of the three sides receives what it read?

choices.text: The real resources, to match the state
choices.why: A refresh-only apply changes nothing in AWS.

choices.text: The configuration, to match AWS
choices.why: Terraform never writes `.tf` files.

choices.text: Only the state, recording what AWS has now
choices.why: Right: it accepts that the world moved, without deciding yet which side wins.

choices.text: Both the state and AWS, to undo the colleague's change
choices.why: Undoing the change is what a plain `apply` does.

prompt: The `web` group's rules are written as separate `aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule` resources, one for 443. A colleague adds port 22 by hand. What does the next plan show?
hint: Which rules does each rule resource compare?

choices.text: A change removing port 22 from the group
choices.why: That happens with inline `ingress` blocks, where the group owns the whole list.

choices.text: No changes
choices.why: Yes. Each rule resource compares only itself; a rule nobody declared is invisible.

choices.text: An error, because two rules now overlap
choices.why: Ports 22 and 443 do not overlap, and drift is not an error.

choices.text: A new rule resource to be imported automatically
choices.why: Terraform does not import on its own; lesson 8 shows import as a deliberate step.

prompt: Why was the state bucket created with the aws CLI instead of in `main.tf`?
hint: What would the very first `init` need?

choices.text: Terraform cannot create S3 buckets
choices.why: It can; the problem is storing its own state in one it creates.

choices.text: Buckets created by the CLI are encrypted and Terraform's are not
choices.why: Encryption is a setting, whoever creates the bucket.

choices.text: The backend needs the bucket to exist before init, and a destroy would delete it
choices.why: Right. So it is made once, outside, by hand or by a small configuration with local state.

choices.text: The CLI is faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

prompt: Ana wants `bucket = var.state_bucket` in the backend block. What happens?
hint: When is the backend configured, compared with the rest?

choices.text: It works once the variable has a default
choices.why: Defaults do not help: no variable is evaluated at that point.

choices.text: It is refused, and the value goes in `-backend-config`
choices.why: Yes. The backend is set up before anything else is evaluated.

choices.text: It works, but only with the local backend
choices.why: No backend block can refer to variables.

choices.text: Terraform asks for the value interactively at every plan
choices.why: That is what a missing ordinary variable does, not a backend.

prompt: Put the steps of moving the shop's state into S3 in order.
hint: The bucket cannot come from the configuration it serves.
items: Create the bucket and turn on versioning
Check `terraform state list`, then delete the local leftovers
trap: Deleting the local file before the migration leaves nothing to migrate.

prompt: With `use_lockfile = true`, where does the S3 backend keep its lock?
hint: Look at the bucket listing while the apply waits.

choices.text: In a DynamoDB table named in the backend block
choices.why: That was the older way, `dynamodb_table`, now deprecated.

choices.text: In a field inside `terraform.tfstate`
choices.why: The state has no lock field; the lock is a separate object.

choices.text: In `.terraform/` on the machine running the apply
choices.why: A local file could not stop another machine.

choices.text: In a second object beside the state, its key ending in `.tflock`
choices.why: Yes, `shop/terraform.tfstate.tflock`, beside the state.

prompt: Which HTTP status code did S3 return when the second run tried to take the lock?
hint: It is printed beside `PreconditionFailed`.

prompt: Why does a plain `terraform plan` take the lock, though it changes nothing in AWS?
hint: What would it read if an apply were halfway through writing?

choices.text: So that it never reads a state being written
choices.why: Right: a plan built on half a state describes a world that never existed.

choices.text: Because a plan saves itself in the bucket
choices.why: A plan writes nothing to the bucket unless you save it yourself with `-out`, and then locally.

choices.text: To reserve the right to apply within the next hour
choices.why: The lock is released when the plan exits.

choices.text: Because S3 refuses reads of an unlocked object
choices.why: S3 knows nothing about Terraform's lock; the lock is a convention between runs.

prompt: A `terraform plan` fails on a lock whose `Who` is a CI runner. Which of these should happen before anyone runs `force-unlock`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The danger is a second writer beside a live one.

choices.text: Confirm the CI job that took it is no longer running
choices.why: Yes: a slow job still holds a valid lock.

choices.text: Note the lock's `ID` from the error
choices.why: Yes; `force-unlock` takes that ID.

choices.text: Delete the state object so the next run starts clean
choices.why: That is losing the state, and the duplicate network that follows.

choices.text: Rerun the plan with `-lock=false` to see whether it works
choices.why: That skips the protection instead of finding out whether it is still needed.

prompt: What does `encrypt = true` in the backend block protect the state against?
hint: Think of who is still allowed to read the object.

choices.text: Someone the bucket policy lets in
choices.why: S3 decrypts for anyone allowed to read; the policy is what keeps people out.

choices.text: Reading it off S3's own disks
choices.why: Yes, encryption at rest, and nothing more.

choices.text: A password showing in plan output
choices.why: Screen output is a different leak, the subject of lesson 12.

choices.text: Two runs writing at once
choices.why: That is the lock's job.

prompt: Ana runs `terraform state push old.tfstate` with a version two writes old. What happens?
hint: Compare the serials.

choices.text: It is refused: serial 1 cannot replace serial 3
choices.why: Right, and only `-force` overrides that check.

choices.text: The old state becomes current and the next plan undoes recent changes
choices.why: That would happen with `-force`; without it the push is refused.

choices.text: S3 creates a new version and keeps the current one as latest
choices.why: Nothing reaches S3: Terraform refuses before writing.

choices.text: Terraform merges the two states
choices.why: States are never merged; one replaces the other or nothing happens.

prompt: Which of these protect the shop's state bucket, as the lesson sets it up? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three different failures, three defences.

choices.text: Versioning, so an older state can be fetched
choices.why: Yes; every write is still in the bucket.

choices.text: Blocking public access
choices.why: Yes; it stops a later policy or ACL publishing it.

choices.text: Committing a copy of the state to git each day
choices.why: Copies in git are stale states and leaked secrets.

choices.text: A policy naming who may use the bucket
choices.why: Yes; the bucket's permissions are the state's permissions.

choices.text: Letting every developer list the bucket
choices.why: That hands them every secret in every state there.

prompt: A run of `terraform apply` with the S3 backend: put what happens in order.
hint: The lock comes before any read.
items: Read the state and refresh each id from AWS
Show the plan and wait for yes
Change AWS and write the new state
trap: Reading the state before taking the lock is the window the lock exists to close.

prompt: A new CI job checks out the repository, which has no `backend.tf`, and runs `terraform apply -auto-approve`. Ana's state is local on her laptop. What does the job do?
hint: Which state does the job read?

choices.text: Creates a second copy of every resource
choices.why: Yes. With no state it plans everything as missing: the clone's duplicate network again.

choices.text: Fails on the lock Ana's laptop holds
choices.why: A local state's lock is on Ana's disk; the job cannot see it.

choices.text: Downloads Ana's state over SSH and reports no changes
choices.why: Terraform only reads the backend it is configured with.

choices.text: Refuses to run, because the lineage does not match
choices.why: There is no state to compare lineages with; it starts a new one.

prompt: A plan shows `aws_subnet.public_a will be destroyed` and `aws_subnet.a will be created`, and nobody changed the subnet. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Two addresses for one subnet.

choices.text: The subnet drifted and AWS changed its CIDR
choices.why: Drift on an attribute shows as an update or a replacement of one address, not two addresses.

choices.text: The provider was upgraded and renamed the resource type
choices.why: The type is `aws_subnet` on both lines; only the name differs.

choices.text: Somebody ran `state mv` and the file was not renamed
choices.why: Yes, the half-way point the lesson showed; renaming the block in `main.tf` gives `No changes`.

choices.text: The state file is corrupted and must be restored from a backup
choices.why: A corrupted state fails to load; this one loaded and planned.

prompt: After the migration to S3, which of these are true of Ana's working directory? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the `ls -l` and the `state list` after the migration.

choices.text: `terraform.tfstate` is empty
choices.why: Yes, zero bytes.

choices.text: `terraform state list` reads from the bucket
choices.why: Yes; nothing local is involved any more.

choices.text: The backups are refreshed on every apply
choices.why: They are leftovers of the local backend, and Ana deletes them.

choices.text: A clone with `backend.tf` plans `No changes`
choices.why: Yes; it reads the same state.

choices.text: `.gitignore` must now allow `*.tfstate`
choices.why: The state is in S3; nothing about it belongs in git.
